fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. I think the simplest way to put it is that usefulness is almost never about raw capability in isolation. If you look at the people who help us most in our lives, a good collaborator, a good doctor, a good advisor, what makes them valuable is not that they know more than a textbook. It is that they know us. They remember what we tried last time, what we care about, what we already understand, and what we tend to get wrong.

Right now most AI assistants are, in a sense, extremely knowledgeable strangers. Every conversation starts from zero. You have to re-explain your codebase, your research direction, your constraints, your preferences, and the model will give you a perfectly reasonable generic answer. But generic is exactly the problem. The marginal value of an assistant comes from how specific it can be to you, and specificity requires context that accumulates over time.

There is also something I find interesting from a modeling perspective. We spend enormous effort scaling pretraining so that models absorb the world's general knowledge. But the information that actually determines whether a response is helpful for a particular person is tiny in comparison, and it is not in the pretraining data at all. It lives in the interaction history. So the bottleneck for usefulness has shifted. It is not about how much the model knows in general. It is about whether the right few kilobytes about you are available at inference time, and whether the model can use them well.

And I think memory changes the nature of the relationship, not just the quality of individual answers. If an assistant remembers that I prefer a certain style of explanation, or that I was debugging a training instability two weeks ago, then it can be proactive rather than reactive. It can connect things. It can say, this looks like the same issue you hit before. That is the difference between a tool you query and something closer to a collaborator.

Of course, this raises hard questions. What should be remembered, what should be forgotten, how do you avoid the model building a wrong picture of someone and then being confidently wrong about them for months. I do not think we have good answers yet. But I think if you ask what the next big jump in perceived usefulness will come from, my bet is that it comes less from a smarter base model and more from the model knowing who it is talking to.

opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, I think it comes down to the difference between intelligence and usefulness. Those are related, but they're not the same thing.

Today's models are already very capable. They can write code, solve math problems, and explain almost anything. But every new conversation starts from zero. It's like hiring a brilliant consultant who has amnesia every morning. They're smart, but you spend the first twenty minutes re-explaining who you are, what you're working on, what you tried last week, and what you care about. That overhead adds up, and honestly a lot of people just don't bother. So the assistant ends up giving generic answers, because it only has a generic picture of you.

Think about what makes a really good human assistant, or a good collaborator, or even a good doctor. Their raw intelligence matters, but much of their value comes from accumulated context. They know your history. They know your preferences. They remember that you tried something and it didn't work. They can anticipate what you need before you ask. That's what memory and personal context give you, and I'd argue that as base capabilities keep improving, context becomes the real bottleneck. The marginal gain from a slightly smarter model is getting smaller for most everyday tasks. The gain from a model that actually knows you is still huge.

There's also a deeper research point. Right now most of what we call "memory" is fairly crude. We stuff things into a long context window, or we retrieve some notes, or we keep a summary file. That works to some degree, but it isn't really how memory works in people. Humans don't re-read their whole life every time they make a decision. We consolidate, we abstract, we forget the irrelevant details and keep the patterns. So I think there's a lot of interesting work to do on how a system should decide what to remember, how to compress it, and how to update its understanding of a person over time. That's closer to continual learning than to just a bigger context window.

And of course it comes with real responsibilities. The more an assistant knows about you, the more useful it is, but also the more sensitive that data becomes. So privacy, user control, and being able to see and edit what the system remembers all have to be part of the design from the start. But I do think an assistant without memory will always feel like a tool, while one with good memory starts to feel like a collaborator.

fable-5.text:
Thanks for having me, Ravid. So the way I think about it is: if you look at what makes a human assistant actually valuable, it's almost never raw intelligence alone. It's the accumulated context. A great assistant knows your preferences, remembers what you decided last month and why, knows which explanations worked for you and which didn't. They don't start from zero every morning.

Current language models are in a strange position where they're incredibly capable in the moment, but they're essentially amnesiac. Every conversation begins from a blank slate, and whatever you taught the model yesterday — your coding conventions, your writing style, the constraints of your project — is just gone. So users end up re-explaining the same things over and over, and the model keeps making the same mistakes it was already corrected on. That's a huge tax on usefulness, and I'd argue it caps how much trust people are willing to place in these systems.

There's also a more fundamental point. Personalization is what turns a general-purpose model into *your* assistant. Two users can ask the literally identical question and the right answer can be different — one is an expert who wants a terse technical response, the other is a student who needs the background filled in. Without memory of who you're talking to, the model has to aim at some average user, and the average user is nobody.

What I find interesting as a researcher is that memory is not just an engineering add-on, like bolting a database onto the model. There are real open questions: what should be remembered versus forgotten, how do you consolidate many interactions into something compact and useful, how do you keep memories from becoming stale or even wrong as the world changes. It touches on continual learning, on retrieval, on how you represent knowledge about a person over time. And of course there's a privacy dimension — the more an assistant remembers, the more carefully you have to think about where that information lives and who controls it.

So to me, memory is central because the frontier is shifting. The models are already smart enough for most everyday tasks; the bottleneck — no pun intended for your show — is increasingly context. The assistants that feel genuinely useful over the next few years will be the ones that learn you, not just the ones that know things.

opus-5.text:
For me it comes down to a pretty simple observation: the models we have now are already smarter than they are useful. If you give one a self-contained problem — a math competition question, a coding puzzle, write me a function that does X — it does extremely well. But most of what people actually want help with isn't self-contained. It's embedded in a situation that the model knows nothing about.

I think of it like hiring. If you bring in a brilliant new researcher, they're not productive on day one. Not because they're not smart, but because they don't know what your lab is working on, what you already tried and abandoned two years ago, which reviewer comments you care about, how your advisor likes things framed. The ramp-up isn't about intelligence, it's about context accumulation. And right now every conversation with an assistant is day one. Forever. You're constantly re-onboarding the same brilliant stranger.

And there's an asymmetry in where the value is. Generic advice is basically free now — it's abundant, it's commoditized. What's scarce is advice that knows your constraints. "Should I use this architecture" has no answer in a vacuum; it depends on your compute budget, your deadline, what your collaborators are comfortable maintaining. A model without that has to either ask twenty clarifying questions or hedge into uselessness, and both of those are bad experiences.

The thing I'd add, which is maybe more of a researcher's complaint, is that we've systematically under-measured this. Benchmarks are made of self-contained problems because those are easy to score. So we've been optimizing hard on the axis we can measure while the actual bottleneck for everyday usefulness sits somewhere else. I don't think the answer is more raw capability on those benchmarks. I think a model that's slightly less capable but actually remembers who you are would feel dramatically more useful to most people, and that gap is only going to widen.

sonnet-5.5.text:
I think it comes down to the gap between a model that's smart in general and an assistant that's useful to you in particular. Today's models are already very capable at lots of tasks. But when I ask for help, a lot of what makes the answer good is stuff that isn't in the prompt: what I'm working on, what I've already tried, how I like things written, who the people in my life are, what I decided last week and why. Without that, I have to re-explain everything every time, and that's a real cost. It's like working with a brilliant colleague who gets amnesia every morning.

So the bottleneck often isn't intelligence, it's context. If the model knows my history and preferences, a short, vague request can turn into the right action. And it compounds. The more it remembers, the less I have to specify, and the more I can delegate. That's when it starts to feel like an assistant rather than a search box with better answers.

I also think it's hard, and not just because of privacy. You have to decide what to store, how to retrieve the right piece at the right time, and how to update it when things change. Remembering everything isn't the goal. Remembering the right things is. A bad memory can be worse than none, if it keeps surfacing outdated or irrelevant stuff. So I see it as a core capability that we're still figuring out.

haiku-5.5.text:
I think it comes down to the difference between answering a question and helping a person. A lot of what makes a good collaborator is that they already know your situation: what you've tried, what you care about, how you like to work. Today most assistants start from zero every time, so you spend effort re-explaining yourself, and the help you get is generic. Memory lets the assistant build up a picture of you over weeks and months, and that's where the usefulness really compounds.

But I don't think more memory is automatically better. Remembering the wrong thing, or remembering something stale, can be worse than remembering nothing, because the assistant acts on it confidently. So the hard part is deciding what's worth keeping, when to bring it up, and how the user can see and correct it. I'd want the memory to be legible, something you can inspect and edit, not a black box that quietly shapes your results.

There's also a privacy question that I think people underweight. Personal context is valuable precisely because it's sensitive, so the design has to make the tradeoff explicit rather than hiding it in defaults.

astra-6.text:
I think an assistant becomes much more useful when it understands the context behind what you’re asking. What are you working on? What do you already know? What are your preferences and constraints? The same question can have very different useful answers depending on those things.

Without memory, you have to reconstruct that context every time. You explain your project, explain what you’ve tried, explain how you want help. That’s a lot of work for the person using the assistant. If it can remember the relevant parts of previous conversations, you can build on what you’ve already done together.

And I think the key word is relevant. Remembering everything doesn’t automatically make an assistant helpful. It needs to use the right context at the right time, recognize that your circumstances can change, and let you correct what it remembers. That’s what would make it feel like an ongoing collaboration.

I think a lot of usefulness comes from understanding the person you’re helping. If I ask an assistant for advice, the answer depends on what I’m working on, what I’ve already tried, what I know, and what my preferences are. Those things are hard to explain from scratch every time.

Memory lets that understanding accumulate. The assistant can remember a decision we made, connect today’s question to an ongoing project, and give an answer that fits my situation. That also reduces the effort of using it. If I have to reconstruct all the background for every question, I’m doing a lot of the work myself.

So I see personal context as a big part of making an assistant useful over time. You want a collaborator that develops a shared understanding with you—and whose memory you can correct when your circumstances or preferences change.

luna-5.6.text:
I think an assistant becomes genuinely useful when it can build continuity with you. Without memory, every interaction starts from zero: you have to repeat your goals, preferences, and constraints, and the assistant can only react to the immediate request. Personal context lets it understand not just what you’re asking, but why you’re asking and how the answer should fit into your life or work. It can adapt to your style, remember decisions you’ve made, and help maintain momentum over time.

But that memory has to be understandable and controllable. People should know what the system remembers, be able to correct or delete it, and decide what kinds of information it may use. The goal isn’t to create a system that knows everything about you; it’s to create one that remembers the context you choose to share, so each interaction can be more helpful without taking away your agency.
